Inside Boston’s North End: 15 Best Things to Do & Neighborhood Guide!

Last Updated on July 31, 2026 by Kate Storm
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 25:01
Instaread

As one of the most historic, picturesque, and fascinating neighborhoods in Boston, the North End is bound to delight most visitors… and that’s without even considering the pervasive scents of pasta sauce and pastries that haunt many of its streets!

Colloquially known as Boston’s Little Italy (among tourists, at least, not so much among the locals), the North End of today is best known for its Italian restaurants, pastry shops, and famous historic sites.

In fact, the North End in Boston is home to 3 of the 16 official Freedom Trail stops!

Add in beautiful architecture and a minuscule 0.36 square mile footprint that is close to many of the other best things to do in Boston, and it’s no surprise that the North End is widely considered a must-see Boston travel destination!

We love visiting the North End, and have been lucky enough to stop by many times over the years, including during our now-traditional annual trip to Greater Boston (having family in the area is an excellent excuse to visit).

Planning a trip to Boston and wondering whether to include the North End? That’s an easy yes!

Here are the best things to do in the North End, plus our tips for making the most of your visit.

Want to Explore the North End the Easy Way?

Planning a last-minute trip to the North End?

We will cover all the best things to do in the North End in much more detail below, including more restaurant and pastry recommendations than can likely fit into one vacation… but to get you started, here are a couple of extremely well-reviewed tours that will show you the best of the North End fast (and without having to plan much yourself):

  • North End Italian Flavors & Heritage Food Tour (a little bit of everything that makes the North End food scene special!)
  • Boston Freedom Trail History Walking Tour (excellent overview that wraps up in the North End, so you can get acquainted with the neighborhood through a guide and then explore more yourself)

Wondering if you should base yourself in the North End? We generally don’t recommend it, but here are a few spots close by that are worth considering:

  • Canopy By Hilton Boston Downtown (hyper-convenient location near Haymarket, multiple T stops, the North End & Faneuil Hall)
  • Boston Marriott Long Wharf (next door to the aquarium, the North End, the water, and a T stop, plus a playground if you’re traveling with kids!)
  • Boston Yacht Haven (modern, airy rooms & right on the water)

15 Best Things to Do in the North End, Boston

Walk the Freedom Trail through the North End.

Without a doubt, the portion of the Freedom Trail that runs through the neighborhood is a must-see in Boston’s North End!

READ NEXT
55 Best Things to Do in Boston (+ Travel Tips!)

You can view the official route here, which in the North End is mostly along Hanover Street and Hull Street (with a few other twists and turns).

Prefer a live guide? This wildly popular Freedom Trail tour includes the North End and actually wraps up there, so you can explore the neighborhood independently after learning about the nitty gritty history (and working up an appetite).

No matter how you choose to explore, though, the most important thing to know is that 3 of the 16 official Freedom Trail stops are in the North End, including:

The Paul Revere House

The Midnight Ride of Paul Revere is one of the most enduring stories of the early American Revolution in Massachusetts, and in the North End, you can visit the hero’s house!

While the true story behind the midnight ride is a bit more complex than the poem, Revere was indeed a brave Son of Liberty who undertook a dangerous overnight ride to warn the patriots in Lexington of the incoming British troops.

READ NEXT
2 Days in Boston: The Ultimate Weekend in Boston Itinerary

His former home, while fascinating and furnished in part with items belonging to the Revere family, actually stretches back even earlier in history to the 1600s!

I loved my tour of the house: it’s small and brief, but very well-done and features knowledgeable interpreters in every room who are eager to answer questions.

As of 2026, tickets are $6.00 per adult. Solo travelers, note that the card minimum is $10.00 and come with cash!

You can check updated prices and hours (they vary seasonally, like so many places in Boston) on the official website.

The Old North Church & Crypt

“One if by land, two if by sea…”: if you remember the story of Paul Revere using lanterns hung from a church tower to alert patriots which route the British were using, well, this is the church in question!

READ NEXT
25 Incredible Places to Visit in New England

Located just a short walk from Paul Revere’s home, the Old North Church dates to 1723 and in addition to being a popular Freedom Trail stop, is still an active Episcopal parish.

The most popular way to tour the church is to go on a self-guided tour of the sanctuary and (small, but interesting) crypt. Alternatively, you can also added on a guided tour of the bell chamber at specific times.

Their website has a breakdown of the different ticket types, along with hours of operation.

It took us many trips to Boston to finally go inside, and we really enjoyed our look around!

However, I wouldn’t necessarily recommend going inside every church on the Freedom Trail if you only have a short time in Boston, and instead choosing 1-2 of them (and Park Street Church is free to visit).

Copp’s Hill Burying Ground (& the Spite House)

Dating to 1659, Copp’s Hill is the biggest colonial burying ground in Boston, and the third Freedom Trail stop in the North End.

In addition to being home to plenty of notable occupants, Copp’s Hill Burying Ground also boasts gorgeous views of Charlestown (including the Bunker Hill Monument) in the distance.

Looking in the opposite direction from Charlestown, you can see a very different point of interest: the Spite House, also known as the Skinny House, which boasts a classic tale of (petty) revenge between its narrow walls.

As the story goes, two brothers inherited land from their father. While one was away serving in the American Civil War, the other brother built a large home, taking over part of the soldier’s inheritance.

READ NEXT
15+ Delightful Day Trips From Boston (By Train, Car, or Tour!)

When the soldier returned home, he built the “Spite House”–incredibly skinny, and yet incredibly effective at blocking his brother’s view.

The legitimacy of the story is somewhat questionable, and the Spite House of course isn’t part of the Freedom Trail, but it sure is a classic Boston tale!

Explore Boston’s Italian-American food scene in the North End by sitting down for a meal.

If there’s one thing you should absolutely prioritize when exploring the North End, it’s eating!

READ NEXT
Planning Your First Trip to NYC: Bucket List + Travel Tips!

The North End’s Italian-American restaurants are legendary to the point of oversaturation: you can’t throw a stone along Hanover Street without hitting at least one.

Not all the restaurants live up to the hype, of course. This is a very tourist-centered neighborhood, and tourist traps abound when choosing where to eat!

We highly, highly recommend researching where you want to eat in advance, and ideally, making a reservation at least a couple days ahead of time.

Within the North End, we particularly loved our experiences at both Ristorante Euno and Tresca (pictured above: everything was delicious, but their house special of chicken parm made with vodka sauce was a standout!).

Not in the mood for Italian? Neptune Oyster is also extremely popular for good reason, and we really enjoyed our meal there!

READ NEXT
What's a Boston Duck Tour Really Like? (We Took Our Toddler!)

Looking for something with less of a time commitment?

If so, Regina Pizzeria is legendary (though they have plenty of locations outside the North End as well), and Italian subs from places like Monica’s Mercato and Bricco Salumeria & Pasta Shop are excellent for sampling the flavors of the North End without settling in for a long meal.

… or by enjoying an in-depth food tour on the go!

Don’t want to choose between pizza, pasta, pane, and pastries? You don’t have to on this wildly popular food tour that covers them all!

If you want to try a little bit of everything that makes the North End food scene special, a food tour is a fantastic way to get an efficient overview of what’s on offer, while exploring some local history and gathering some behind-the-scenes knowledge along the way.

We’re big fans of food tours around the world (we’ve been on dozens!), and I think that the North End is easily one of the best neighborhoods in Boston to enjoy one in.

Book your North End food and culture tour today!

Stroll down Hanover Street.

The North End’s main drag, so to speak, is simultaneously busy and beautiful. It’s also a North End must-see!

READ NEXT
15 Amazing Things to Do in Acadia National Park

Luckily, seeing it isn’t hard to accomplish: not only is there a good chance you enter the North End through Hanover Street, but many of the neighborhood’s most iconic institutions, including Mike’s Pastry and Modern Pastry, are located here.

And, if you turn right off of Hanover Street, you’ll find…

Snap a photo with Paul Revere at the Paul Revere Mall.

The shady, peaceful Paul Revere Mall connects Hanover Street to the Old North Church over on Unity Street via a beautiful brick park/square.

READ NEXT
13 Epic East Coast Cities for Weekend Getaways

It’s a great place to rest your feet, maybe enjoy a pastry (more on that in a moment!), soak up some views, and… take a photo with Paul Revere himself!

The imposing statue of Revolutionary War hero Paul Revere is a classic North End sightseeing stop, and a great lead-in to visiting the Old North Church (or Paul Revere’s house, which is a short walk away in the opposite direction).

Grab some of Boston’s celebrated Italian-American pastries.

It’s not a trip to the North End without some Italian(-American) desserts!

There are plenty of options to choose from, but, well, some of them are more iconic than others (and ironically, the most famous of them all is actually the newest of the shops we’re highlighting, as it was established in “only” 1946).

In order of fame, here are 4 places we suggest considering:

READ NEXT
4 Days in NYC: The Ultimate (Massive) 4 Days in New York Itinerary
  • Mike’s Pastry: The most famous of these spots, which usually features a long line! If you get lucky and see it without a line (we did), grab some cannoli. If there is a line, well… it’s good, but I’d order online or visit another location instead.
  • Modern Pastry: The “alternative” to Mike’s Pastry that has now become very well-known in its own right. The cannoli are delicious!
  • Bova’s Bakery: My personal favorite for desserts in general. The sponges are an absolute standout, we loved the Boston cream, German chocolate, and vanilla cupcake (seriously), but everything we’ve tried has been amazing.
  • Caffé Vittoria: If you want to sit down inside and enjoy a peaceful coffee-and-dessert that feels almost like being in Europe if you squint, this is the place for you! We love the atmosphere here.

If you opt for one of the first three options, consider walking a bit and grabbing a shaded bench along the Paul Revere Mall in order to enjoy them!

It’s one of the most peaceful spots in the immediate vicinity for a snack, and you’ll probably be planning to visit anyway.

Note that with the exception of Bova Bakery, which takes cards, all of these establishment are cash-only.

Shop at an Italian market in the North End.

Looking for artisanal pasta, delicious sauces, imported traditional balsamic vinegar, olive oil, or other Italian specialties?

Add an Italian market to your list of places to visit in the North End!

READ NEXT
17 Fun Weekend Getaways from Boston

Salumeria Italiana is an expansive, popular standby for good reason.

Bricco Salumeria & Pasta Shop (which also boasts their own panetteria) is smaller but lovely, and you can even grab a sub before or after shopping.

Monica’s Mercato is mostly focused on their popular sandwiches, but they stock some specialty products as well.

Stop the oldest public square in Boston.

In the oldest public square in Boston, you can sit under the shade of a tree and watch the world go by… as visitors and residents have been doing in this spot in one way or another for almost 400 years!

Dating to the 1630s, North Square is home to interesting art installations (including a bronze, birds-eye-view map of the North End itself) and is lined with several notable buildings as well as the adjacent Rachel Revere Square.

One spot on the square stands head and shoulders above the rest when it comes to fame, though: North Square is where you’ll find Paul Revere’s House.

Pay a visit to the brand-new North End Historical Museum.

This summer, I was walking through the North End when I spotted the sign for the North End Historical Museum… and immediately wondered how I could have missed it for all these years.

READ NEXT
21+ Dreamy East Coast Beach Towns (Perfect for Summer Getaways)

As it turns out, though, I hadn’t: the North End Historical Museum, which will explore the neighborhood’s 400 year history and the people who crafted it, opened for the first time in July 2026!

The museum is now open Tuesday-Sunday, 10:30-5:00, and you can confirm details on their website and Instagram.

Wander some of the most beautiful streets in Boston’s North End.

At only 0.36 square miles, the North End may be small, but it is incredibly densely packed with weaving, charming streets to wander down.

And, if you have time, you should definitely add some time to your North End itinerary to wander semi-aimlessly among them!

READ NEXT
15 Wicked Fun Quotes About Boston

A few beautiful spots to keep an eye out for include Salem Street, Prince Street, Charter Street, and Public Alley 101.

The corner where Salem and Prince Streets meet is particularly photogenic, and there’s a good chance you’ve seen it in photos before when planning your trip to the North End! You’ll also find Monica’s Mercato and Bova’s Bakery right here, making this intersection an excellent stop for several reasons.

One beautiful Boston street you won’t find in the North End? Famous Acorn Street, which is over in Beacon Hill.

Check out the colorful All Saint’s Way.

Like checking out quirky, unusual points of interest as you explore?

If so, be sure to stroll between 4 and 8 Battery Street on your North End walking tour.

READ NEXT
USA Bucket List: 50 Best Places to Visit in the US

Here, you’ll find a tiny alley bursting with photos and color from all directions, all thanks to one man: Peter Baldassari, who has been decorating this small space with pictures and art dedicated to saints for decades.

Rumor has it that Baldassari will sometimes give tours, so if you’re lucky enough to spot him offering one, be sure to stop and say hello!

Long ago, we first stumbled upon All Saint’s Way completely accidentally, with no idea that it was something of a local attraction, and it of course immediately caught our eyes. I’ll always have a soft spot for it for that reason.

Attend one of the North End’s famous feasts.

Summer brings endless reasons to visit Boston, and the North End’s legendary feasts are one of them!

READ NEXT
21+ Dreamy East Coast Beach Towns (Perfect for Summer Getaways)

These annual, multi-day events are generally held in honor of a specific saint, and the festivals often have roots dating back to Italy.

Think music, processions/parades, games, dancing in the streets, and of course, lots and lots of food!

Saint Anthony’s Feast, held every August and nicknamed the “Feast of All Feasts”, is the largest and most celebrated of them all, but there are several incredible feasts held in the North End each summer.

Fun Things to Do Near Boston’s North End

While the North End itself may be small, many of the other top things to do in Boston are located only a short walk away!

In and around Haymarket (and its convenient T stop), you’ll find the Boston Public Market, Rose Kennedy Greenway, the New England Holocaust Memorial, and aesthetic Union Street, which is home to the Bell in Hand Tavern and Union Oyster House.

City Hall, widely considered an exceptionally ugly building, and the City Hall Plaza Playground are also nearby. Our 2-year-old was a big fan of the playground on our most recent trip, and we learned after the fact that the biggest slide there went viral a few years back (if you’ve heard of the Boston Cop Slide, this is the one).

Keep heading south, and you’ll be at Faneuil Hall before you know it.

Just southeast of Faneuil Hall, right on the water, is the excellent New England Aquarium, where the resident penguins have always a been a huge hit with our family.

Long Wharf, right next to the aquarium, is also a popular launch point for ferries, duck tours (lots of fun, here’s our review), whale watching excursions, and sightseeing cruises like this.

Should You Stay in the North End?

While the North End is easily one of the best neighborhoods in Boston to visit, it’s not generally the best place to stay!

Not only is the North End extremely residential (you won’t find big hotels here, and rental apartments are regulated and limited), but its lack of a T station means that it’s not the most convenient neighborhood to get in and out of during a Boston sightseeing trip.

READ NEXT
3 Days in Philly: The Perfect Weekend in Philadelphia Itinerary

If you want to stay close to the North End without sacrificing convenience, here are a few well-reviewed places where we’d personally consider basing ourselves:

  • Canopy By Hilton Boston Downtown (hyper-convenient location near Haymarket, multiple T stops, the North End & Faneuil Hall)
  • Boston Marriott Long Wharf (next door to the aquarium, the North End, the water, and a T stop, plus a playground if you’re traveling with kids!)
  • Boston Yacht Haven (modern, airy rooms & right on the water)

Tips for Visiting the North End in Boston

Arrive on foot, and plan to walk in the North End.

The North End is small, residential, and very urban. In other words, it’s a place to explore on your feet!

READ NEXT
How to Plan the Perfect Boston to Plymouth Day Trip

You won’t even see many things like electric scooters around here: the sidewalks are crowded and fairly narrow, and the streets small.

The absolute best way to visit the North End is to arrive on foot and plan to stay that way throughout your visit.

Come hungry (and with a plan).

While there is some excellent traditional sightseeing in the North End, above all other things, this is a place to eat!

We strongly recommend coming prepared, with a restaurant and/or pastry shop picked out and, in the case of a restaurant, reservations made (especially if you’re visiting on a weekend and/or in the popular summer and fall sightseeing months).

READ NEXT
How to Have a Fun Weekend in Baltimore: Itinerary + Tips

Want to visit somewhere like Monica’s Mercato that can attract long lines? Consider planning to eat at an off-time, rather than peak lunch or dinner hours.

Want to skip all the planning and just eat? Booking a food tour like this is a fantastic way to sample the best of North End cuisine without having to worry about scheduling things yourself!

Book your North End food tour today!

The Paul Revere Mall is a great place to enjoy a pastry.

I mentioned this above, but it bears repeating!

The Paul Revere Mall is shaded, fairly peaceful (you’ll see tour groups, of course, but it’s set back from traffic), and has seating along the edges, making it an excellent place to rest your feet and enjoy a pastry before continuing on with your sightseeing.

It also happens to be a very short walk away from every bakery/dessert shop that I recommended above.

Leave time to meander.

While there are some excellent North End attractions, ultimately, visiting Boston’s Little Italy is as much about wandering around and enjoying the atmosphere as it is about traditional sightseeing (though really, it’s more about food than either of those).

READ NEXT
33 Stunning Places to Visit in Summer in the USA (Vacation Spots Not to Miss!)

When sketching out your Boston itinerary, I’d recommend leaving at least 2 hours beyond the time you plan to be eating to enjoy the North End.

That should give you enough time for a walk through some of the neighborhood’s loveliest spots, plus time to hit up a specific attraction or two.

Bring cash!

Definitely come prepared to spend some cash when visiting the North End!

A surprising number of places in the neighborhood are cash-only, including both Mike’s Pastry, Modern Pastry, and many restaurants.

There are lots of ATMs scattered around if you need one, so be ready to use one if needed.

How to Get to Boston’s North End

Wondering how to get to Boston’s North End?

READ NEXT
How to Budget for a Trip: The Easiest Travel Budgeting Method (+ Tips!)

If you’re already sightseeing in the center of Boston, like on a typical weekend trip to the city, there’s a good chance you can just walk there!

However, if you’re coming from further away, you’ll likely need to choose between the train (best) and driving (not ideal, but doable if needed).

Here’s what each option looks like:

By Train

Boston’s subway system, known simply as “the T” is your best bet for getting close enough to the North End to walk in.

The most convenient station is Haymarket (green and orange lines). The Aquarium stop (blue line), Government Center (green and blue lines), and North Station (green and orange lines) also work.

You can browse the MBTA map and schedule here.

By Car

In a perfect world, our best advice for driving to the North End is: don’t do it.

Boston traffic is legendary, North End parking is extremely limited, and all in all it’s a stressful and expenisve idea.

READ NEXT
7+ Epic East Coast USA Road Trip Routes (Itineraries + Travel Tips)

However! We tend to stay outside the center these days (a million thanks to my stepmom’s condo in Greater Boston), so we have had a bit of experience driving in as well.

At the advice of my stepmom, who lived and worked in Boston for 30+ years, we park just outside the North End at Lewis Wharf Parking or the Dock Square Parking Garage. Both are functional, if crowded and pricey.

If you park at Lewis Wharf, you can see the planes taking off and landing across the harbor if you pause to watch for a bit!

Self-Guided North End Walking Tour Itinerary

There are, of course, endless ways to explore Boston’s Little Italy… but if you’re looking for an efficient, self-led walking route, we’ve enjoyed variations on this one many times!

READ NEXT
25 Best Christmas Vacations in the USA

Start by arriving at Haymarket, possibly stopping by Union Street and/or the Boston Public Market before strolling past the Rose Kennedy Greenway and into the North End via Hanover Street.

Make your way down Hanover Street for a bit, and then detour to North Square and check out Paul Revere’s House. The North End Historical Museum is also right around the corner.

From there, double-back to Hanover Street and grab a pastry! Mike’s, Modern, and Caffé Vittoria are all grouped close together on Hanover Street, and if you opt for Bova Bakery, it’s just a short stroll along Prince Street away (and it’ll take you right to the scenic corner of Prince & Salem, too).

From there, head to the Paul Revere Mall to enjoy your sweet treat. A short detour further along Hanover will take you to All Saint’s Way, if you like!

Make your way through the Paul Revere Mall to Old North Church. From there, head to Copp’s Hill Burying Ground to check out your third Freedom Trail stop of the neighborhood.

Afterward, stroll to the corner of Prince and Salem Streets (if you haven’t already seen it), which will put you back in closer proximity to the bulk of the North End’s restaurants.

From there, it’s time to eat! Head over to where you have reservations, or set off on your food tour (though I recommend skipping the pastry stop above if you’re taking the tour!).
